title: Heroin Addiction Treatment in New York and NYSHIP
desc: Understand heroin addiction, evidence-based treatment options like MAT, and how NYSHIP/Empire Plan may cover detox and rehab for New York State employees.
h1: Heroin Addiction Treatment in New York: What NYSHIP Members Should Know
author: NYSHIP Detox Editorial Team
bodyHtml:
Heroin use disorder is a serious, chronic medical condition—and it is treatable. For New York State employees and their dependents enrolled in NYSHIP (the New York State Health Insurance Program), including the Empire Plan, understanding what treatment options exist and how coverage may apply is an important first step toward recovery. This article is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice; please consult a qualified healthcare provider for guidance specific to your situation.

How Heroin Addiction Develops

Heroin is a rapidly acting opioid derived from morphine. According to the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA), heroin binds to opioid receptors in the brain with high affinity, producing an intense but short-lived euphoria followed by drowsiness. Repeated use causes the brain to adapt: tolerance develops, meaning larger amounts are needed to achieve the same effect, and physical dependence follows—where stopping or dramatically reducing use triggers withdrawal.

Heroin use disorder can develop quickly, sometimes within weeks of first use, making early intervention critical. The risk is compounded by the fact that illicit heroin today is frequently contaminated with or entirely replaced by synthetic fentanyl, which is dramatically more potent and unpredictable.

Recognizing the Signs

MedlinePlus, a service of the U.S. National Library of Medicine, identifies common signs of heroin use and dependence:

  • Needle marks, bruising, or track marks on arms (with injection use)
  • Sudden changes in behavior—withdrawal from family or friends, loss of interest in activities
  • Drastic weight loss, poor hygiene, or neglected appearance
  • Drowsiness or “nodding off” at unusual times
  • Flu-like symptoms between uses (early withdrawal: nausea, sweating, muscle aches, anxiety)
  • Financial problems, missing money, or selling possessions
  • Possession of drug paraphernalia such as syringes, spoons, or foil

If you recognize these signs in yourself or someone you care about, reaching out for help as soon as possible can be life-saving. Call the SAMHSA National Helpline at 1-800-662-4357 (free, confidential, 24/7) for immediate assistance locating treatment, or dial 988 for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline if there is an immediate safety concern.

Why Medical Supervision During Detox Is Essential

Heroin withdrawal is not typically life-threatening on its own, but it is profoundly uncomfortable—and the discomfort is one of the primary reasons people return to use before treatment can take hold. A medically supervised opioid addiction treatment program manages withdrawal symptoms with medications that ease cravings and physical distress, dramatically improving the likelihood that a person completes detox and transitions to ongoing care.

The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) emphasizes that detox alone is rarely sufficient—it is the entry point to treatment, not treatment itself. A comprehensive program follows detox with therapy, peer support, and relapse-prevention planning.

Evidence-Based Medications for Heroin Use Disorder

Medication-assisted treatment (MAT) is the gold-standard, evidence-based approach for opioid use disorder and is supported by major medical organizations. Three FDA-approved medications are available:

  • Buprenorphine (Suboxone, Subutex): A partial opioid agonist that reduces cravings and withdrawal without producing the same euphoric effect as heroin. It can be prescribed in an office-based setting by certified providers.
  • Methadone: A long-acting full opioid agonist dispensed through federally regulated opioid treatment programs (OTPs). It has decades of evidence supporting its effectiveness.
  • Naltrexone (Vivitrol): An opioid antagonist that blocks the effects of opioids entirely. Delivered as a monthly injectable, it is a strong option for people who have already completed detox and are highly motivated to remain abstinent.

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), MAT reduces opioid use, decreases overdose deaths, and improves social functioning. Accessing medication-assisted treatment early in recovery significantly increases the likelihood of long-term success.

If naloxone (Narcan) is available, it can be administered in an overdose emergency before EMS arrives to temporarily reverse opioid effects and restore breathing. New York's Good Samaritan Law provides legal protections to people who call 911 in good faith during an overdose—no one should hesitate to call for help.

NYSHIP and Empire Plan Coverage for Heroin Treatment

NYSHIP members enrolled in the Empire Plan or other participating plans may have benefits that apply to medically necessary substance use disorder treatment, including detoxification, inpatient rehabilitation, and outpatient services. Coverage details—including applicable copays, deductibles, and prior authorization requirements—vary by plan and level of care.

Under the federal Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act (MHPAEA), insurance plans that cover substance use disorder treatment must do so on terms no more restrictive than those for comparable medical or surgical benefits. This means NYSHIP plans generally cannot impose day or visit limits on SUD treatment that they would not impose on medical care.

We recommend calling the member services number on the back of your NYSHIP insurance card or contacting your Employee Assistance Program (EAP) to verify your specific benefits before beginning treatment. Our team can also help guide you through the verification process—please call us at 213-321-6518.

Confidentiality Protections for NY State Employees

Many people hesitate to seek treatment out of concern that their employer will find out. Federal law provides strong protections. Records related to substance use disorder treatment are protected by 42 CFR Part 2, a federal regulation that imposes stricter confidentiality standards than standard HIPAA. Your employer, supervisor, or union cannot access your treatment records without your explicit written consent. Seeking help will not automatically jeopardize your employment.

If you need time away from work for treatment, the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) may entitle eligible employees to up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave per year for a serious health condition, which includes substance use disorder treatment.

Finding Help

Recovery from heroin addiction is possible—thousands of New York State employees and their families have done it. The first call is often the hardest, but SAMHSA's National Helpline (1-800-662-4357) and the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline are available 24 hours a day, seven days a week, and are completely free and confidential.

faq.q: Does NYSHIP cover heroin detox and rehab?
faq.a: NYSHIP/Empire Plan members may have benefits for medically necessary substance use disorder treatment, including detox and inpatient or outpatient rehab. Coverage specifics—copays, deductibles, prior authorization—vary by plan. Contact your plan's member services or our team at 213-321-6518 to verify your benefits before starting treatment.

faq.q: Will my employer know if I seek treatment for heroin addiction?
faq.a: No. Federal law (42 CFR Part 2) protects substance use disorder treatment records with stricter confidentiality rules than standard HIPAA. Your employer cannot access your records without your explicit written consent. New York State employees may also be entitled to job-protected FMLA leave for treatment.

faq.q: What is medication-assisted treatment and is it effective for heroin?
faq.a: MAT combines FDA-approved medications—buprenorphine, methadone, or naltrexone—with counseling and support services. According to NIDA and the CDC, MAT significantly reduces illicit opioid use, lowers overdose mortality, and improves long-term recovery outcomes. It is the evidence-based standard of care for opioid use disorder.

faq.q: What should I do if someone is overdosing on heroin?
faq.a: Call 911 immediately. If naloxone (Narcan) is available, administer it right away—it can temporarily reverse an opioid overdose and restore breathing. New York's Good Samaritan Law protects people who call 911 in good faith during an overdose, so do not hesitate to call for help.

title: Employee Assistance Programs and Addiction Help
desc: NY State employees can use their Employee Assistance Program alongside NYSHIP coverage to access confidential addiction assessment, referrals, and treatment support.
h1: Employee Assistance Programs and Addiction Treatment for NY State Employees
author: NYSHIP Detox Editorial Team
bodyHtml:
New York State and government employees have access to a layered set of supports when dealing with addiction — for themselves or a family member. One that is often overlooked is the Employee Assistance Program (EAP). Understanding how EAPs work, and how they fit alongside NYSHIP insurance benefits, can make a real difference in getting help quickly and confidently. This article is general education, not medical or legal advice; confirm the details of your specific program with your HR office or EAP provider.

What Is an Employee Assistance Program?

An EAP is a confidential, employer-sponsored benefit that provides assessment, short-term counseling, and referrals for personal and work-related concerns — including substance use and mental health issues. According to the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), EAPs are an important pathway to connecting workers with appropriate care, particularly in the early stages when someone first recognizes a problem but may not know where to turn.

New York State employees typically have access to the Civil Service EAP, administered through the New York State Department of Civil Service in partnership with union and management programs. EAP counselors provide confidential assessments and referrals at no cost to the employee.

What EAPs Can and Cannot Do

EAPs are designed to connect people with the right care, not to serve as long-term treatment. For addiction concerns, an EAP typically provides:

  • Confidential screening and assessment to help identify whether a substance use disorder is present and what level of care may be appropriate
  • Referrals to treatment, including detox, inpatient programs, intensive outpatient programs, and ongoing counseling
  • Short-term counseling — usually a limited number of sessions — to help stabilize a situation while longer-term care is arranged
  • Coordination with your NYSHIP benefits so that referrals align with in-network providers and covered services
  • Assistance with workplace concerns, such as understanding leave rights or how to navigate a conversation with a supervisor

An EAP counselor cannot substitute for medically supervised detox or extended treatment. For medically necessary care, NYSHIP and Empire Plan insurance is the primary coverage source — not the EAP itself.

How EAP and NYSHIP Work Together

The most effective use of these benefits is usually sequential: contact the EAP first for a confidential assessment and referral, then use your NYSHIP benefits to cover the cost of actual treatment. The EAP helps identify the right level of care, and our team can assist with a NYSHIP coverage verification to confirm what your plan covers before you begin.

The National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) describes addiction as a treatable, chronic medical condition. Getting a professional assessment — through an EAP or directly through a treatment provider — is an important first step, because it helps match the right level of care to the specific situation. More intensive care, such as inpatient or residential treatment, generally requires insurance authorization, which the EAP referral process can help initiate.

Confidentiality Protections for Employees

Privacy is among the most common concerns for public employees considering help for addiction. EAP records are kept separate from your employment record, and EAP counselors operate under strict confidentiality rules. Substance use treatment records held by federally assisted programs are also protected by federal regulations that, in most circumstances, prevent disclosure to an employer without your explicit written consent. The SAMHSA confidentiality guidance explains these protections in detail. Seeking help through an EAP or NYSHIP benefits generally will not result in your employer being notified.

Other Resources for NY State Employees

In addition to EAP services, New York State employees may have access to union-based resources, Employee Benefits Division assistance, and programs coordinated through the New York State Office of Addiction Services and Supports (OASAS). The MedlinePlus overview of substance use disorders provides clear, plain-language information on what these conditions involve and what treatment generally looks like — useful reading before or after an EAP call or a treatment conversation.

For alcohol use concerns, the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) offers a thorough guide on treatment options. You can also learn what insurance typically covers on our does NYSHIP cover rehab page.

Steps to Get Started

If you or a family member is struggling with addiction, the EAP is one of the lowest-barrier first steps available. You can typically reach your EAP by calling the toll-free number listed in your benefits materials or by contacting your HR office. The call is confidential, and no supervisor approval is required. After an initial assessment, the counselor can help identify appropriate treatment options and coordinate with your NYSHIP coverage. For immediate questions about treatment, our team is available at 213-321-6518.

For free, confidential, 24/7 treatment referrals, call the SAMHSA National Helpline at 1-800-662-4357. If you are in crisis or having thoughts of suicide, call or text the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. Recovery is possible, and the first phone call — to an EAP, a helpline, or a treatment provider — is often the most important step. This content is for educational purposes only and does not constitute medical or legal advice.

faq.q: Can my supervisor find out I contacted the EAP about addiction?
faq.a: No. EAP records are separate from employment records, and counselors operate under strict confidentiality rules. Substance use treatment records also have federal privacy protections that generally prevent employer disclosure without your explicit written consent. This is general education; confirm specifics with your EAP provider or a qualified attorney.

faq.q: Does my EAP cover the cost of addiction treatment?
faq.a: EAPs typically provide assessment, short-term counseling, and referrals at no cost, but they are not a source of insurance coverage for treatment. Medically necessary care — including detox, inpatient rehab, and medication-assisted treatment — is generally covered through your NYSHIP or Empire Plan benefits, subject to plan rules.

faq.q: How do I contact the EAP as a NY State employee?
faq.a: Most NY State employees can reach the EAP through the toll-free number listed in their benefits materials or by contacting their HR office. The call is confidential and does not require supervisor approval. Our team can also help guide you at 213-321-6518.

faq.q: Can the EAP help if I am worried about a family member's addiction?
faq.a: Many EAPs extend services to dependents and family members as well as employees. An EAP counselor can provide guidance, referrals, and support for family members dealing with a loved one's substance use.

title: Mindfulness-Based Relapse Prevention: A NYSHIP Guide
desc: Mindfulness-based relapse prevention (MBRP) builds craving awareness and reduces relapse risk. Evidence-based guidance for NYSHIP members in recovery.
h1: Mindfulness-Based Relapse Prevention: Evidence and Practice for NY State Employees
author: NYSHIP Detox Editorial Team
bodyHtml:
Recovery from addiction is not a single event but an ongoing process — and one of the most practical sets of tools developed to support long-term sobriety draws on mindfulness. Mindfulness-Based Relapse Prevention, commonly called MBRP, is a structured, evidence-based program that teaches people in recovery to recognize and respond to high-risk situations, cravings, and emotional triggers with awareness rather than automatic reaction. For New York State employees using NYSHIP benefits for addiction treatment, understanding MBRP and how it fits into the continuum of care can strengthen the foundation of lasting recovery.

This article is general education, not medical or clinical advice. If you or a loved one is in crisis, call or text 988, or reach the SAMHSA National Helpline at 1-800-662-4357.

What Is Mindfulness-Based Relapse Prevention?

MBRP was developed by researchers at the University of Washington as an integration of mindfulness meditation practices with cognitive-behavioral relapse prevention strategies. It builds on the insight that relapse often unfolds through a predictable chain of events: an internal or external trigger leads to increased craving or emotional discomfort, which leads to a habitual response — and in recovery, that habitual response can be a return to substance use. MBRP intervenes at the point between trigger and response, teaching participants to pause, observe what is happening, and choose a deliberate course of action rather than act on autopilot.

According to the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA), effective addiction treatment must address not just the physical aspects of dependence but also the behavioral and psychological patterns that sustain substance use. MBRP targets exactly these patterns by building a practical skill set that becomes more accessible with regular practice.

The Evidence Base for MBRP

MBRP is not a wellness trend — it has been studied in randomized controlled trials comparing it to standard relapse prevention and standard aftercare. Research published by the University of Washington's Addictive Behaviors Research Center found that participants who completed MBRP showed significantly lower rates of substance use at follow-up compared to standard relapse prevention alone, with particularly strong effects on heavy drug use and craving intensity. The program has been evaluated across alcohol, opioid, and stimulant use disorders.

The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) recognizes mindfulness-based approaches as evidence-supported practices for both substance use disorders and co-occurring mental health conditions such as depression and anxiety. Because depression and anxiety are among the most common drivers of relapse, interventions that address both simultaneously carry real clinical value for people in long-term recovery.

The National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) likewise recognizes that behavioral approaches — particularly those that build coping skills and distress tolerance — are a cornerstone of effective alcohol treatment and sustained relapse prevention.

How MBRP Differs From General Mindfulness

General mindfulness practice — apps, classes, or meditation retreats — can be beneficial for stress and overall wellbeing. MBRP differs in that it is specifically structured around the recovery context. Sessions focus on:

  • Recognizing the early warning signs of a relapse cycle — not just external triggers, but the internal states and thought patterns that precede craving
  • Urge surfing: using breath and body awareness to observe cravings as temporary waves that peak and pass, rather than forces that demand to be acted upon
  • Identifying automatic pilot — the habitual, unexamined mental mode in which relapse most often begins — and replacing it with deliberate, values-based choice
  • Building self-compassion, which reduces the shame spiral that can turn a lapse into a full relapse

This specificity is what gives MBRP its evidence base. The skills are not generic stress-reduction techniques — they are mapped directly to the high-risk moments that people in recovery actually face.

Core MBRP Practices

A standard MBRP program typically runs eight weekly group sessions. Core practices include:

  • Body scan meditation: a systematic, non-judgmental observation of physical sensations that builds the capacity to notice cravings as body-based experiences without acting on them immediately
  • Mindful breathing: a simple anchor practice that can be used in real time during moments of high stress or intense craving
  • SOBER breathing space: a brief, structured pause — Stop, Observe, Breathe, Expand awareness, Respond mindfully — that can be used anywhere, in any high-risk moment
  • Mindful movement: gentle, yoga-based stretching that integrates body awareness with the stress-regulation skills built in seated practice
  • Relapse prevention mapping: using mindfulness skills to identify personal high-risk situations and develop a deliberate, practiced response plan for each one

How MBRP Fits Into NYSHIP-Covered Care

For NY State employees accessing treatment through NYSHIP rehab benefits, MBRP typically appears as a component of intensive outpatient (IOP) programming or as a structured aftercare intervention following residential or inpatient treatment. The federal Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act (MHPAEA) requires most plans, including NYSHIP and the Empire Plan, to cover behavioral health treatment on terms comparable to medical care — which means evidence-based behavioral therapies informed by MBRP are generally a covered benefit when clinically indicated.

To understand what your specific NYSHIP plan covers for outpatient behavioral therapy and aftercare, a free benefits verification is the clearest starting point. Coverage varies by plan type, provider network, and level of care, and our team can walk you through exactly what applies to your situation at no cost and with full confidentiality under HIPAA and 42 CFR Part 2.

According to MedlinePlus, substance use disorders are chronic conditions that benefit from long-term support and evidence-based management. MBRP is designed precisely for this long-term phase — helping people maintain the gains made in formal treatment by building a durable internal skill set rather than relying solely on external supports.

Getting Started

MBRP does not require any prior meditation experience — it is designed to be learned from the ground up, typically within a structured group program guided by a trained clinician. Regular home practice between sessions is a key part of how the skills develop and become reliable in high-risk moments. If you are completing or planning a course of treatment through NYSHIP and want to understand how MBRP can be part of your aftercare plan, our team is ready to help.

Call 213-321-6518 for a free, confidential conversation about your treatment options and NYSHIP coverage. For free, 24/7 treatment support, call the SAMHSA National Helpline at 1-800-662-4357. If you or a loved one is in crisis, call or text 988. This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical or clinical advice.

faq.q: Is mindfulness-based relapse prevention covered by NYSHIP?
faq.a: Evidence-based behavioral therapies for addiction treatment, including MBRP-informed approaches, are generally covered by NYSHIP and the Empire Plan when clinically indicated, under federal mental health parity protections. Specific coverage depends on your plan and provider network. Call 213-321-6518 for a free benefits verification.

faq.q: Do I need meditation experience to participate in MBRP?
faq.a: No. MBRP is designed to be learned from the ground up — no prior meditation experience is required or expected. Sessions introduce practices step by step, and facilitators are trained to work with participants across all experience levels, including those who are skeptical of meditation.

faq.q: How long does a standard MBRP program take?
faq.a: A standard MBRP curriculum consists of eight weekly group sessions, each typically lasting about two hours, often supplemented by brief daily home practice between sessions. Some programs offer condensed or adapted versions. Ask your treatment provider about the specific format available to you.

faq.q: Can MBRP help with anxiety and depression in recovery?
faq.a: MBRP is specifically designed to address the emotional discomfort — including anxiety, low mood, and stress — that commonly drives relapse risk. Research and SAMHSA guidance both recognize mindfulness-based approaches as evidence-supported for co-occurring mood conditions alongside substance use disorders. It is a complement to, not a replacement for, clinical treatment of depression or anxiety.
